# Software Engineering Knowledge Base

> Reference on software engineering and system design for people and AI coding agents.
> One topic per Markdown file; INDEX.md has tags and use cases, glossary.md defines terms.

## apis

- [API versioning and evolution](apis/api-versioning-and-evolution.md): Once clients you do not control depend on your API, every change is a compatibility question.
- [GraphQL](apis/graphql.md): GraphQL is a query language and runtime for APIs where the client sends a query describing the exact shape of data it wants, against a strongly typed schema, usually through one HTTP endpoint.
- [gRPC and Protocol Buffers](apis/grpc-and-protobuf.md): Protocol Buffers (protobuf) is a compact, schema-first binary serialisation format with generated code; gRPC is an RPC framework that uses protobuf over HTTP/2 to give typed unary and streaming calls across languages.
- [Long-running operations and async request-reply](apis/long-running-operations.md): When work takes longer than a client, proxy or load balancer will wait, the API should accept the request, return `202 Accepted` at once with a link to an operation (job) resource, and let the client poll that resource, or receive a callback, until the work succeeds or fails.
- [Pagination, filtering and sorting](apis/pagination-filtering-sorting.md): List endpoints must never return unbounded results.
- [REST API design](apis/rest-api-design.md): REST-style HTTP APIs expose resources (nouns) at stable URLs and manipulate them with standard methods and status codes.
- [Webhooks](apis/webhooks.md): A webhook is an HTTP callback: when something happens in system A, A sends an HTTP POST with an event payload to a URL registered by system B.

## architecture

- [CQRS and event sourcing](architecture/cqrs-and-event-sourcing.md): CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) separates the model that handles writes (commands) from the model(s) that serve reads (queries), so each can be shaped and scaled for its job.
- [Domain-driven design](architecture/domain-driven-design.md): DDD is an approach to software for complicated domains: build a shared language with domain experts, split the problem into bounded contexts, and model the core with entities, value objects and aggregates that enforce business invariants.
- [Event-driven architecture](architecture/event-driven-architecture.md): In an event-driven architecture, components communicate by publishing events (facts about something that happened) to a broker, and interested components react asynchronously.
- [Layered, hexagonal and clean architecture](architecture/layered-hexagonal-clean-architecture.md): These are three related ways to organize code inside one service.
- [Modular monolith](architecture/modular-monolith.md): A modular monolith is one deployable application split into modules that each own one business capability, its data and a small public interface; other modules may use only that interface.
- [Monolith vs microservices](architecture/monolith-vs-microservices.md): A monolith is one deployable unit; microservices are many independently deployable services, each owning its data and one business capability.
- [Serverless architecture](architecture/serverless-architecture.md): Serverless means you run code and use managed services without provisioning or patching servers; the platform scales to demand, including to zero, and bills by use.
- [The twelve-factor app](architecture/twelve-factor-app.md): Twelve-factor is a methodology (from Heroku engineers) for building services that deploy cleanly to cloud platforms, scale horizontally, and minimise divergence between dev and production.

## case-studies

- [Design a chat system](case-studies/design-chat-system.md): A chat system delivers messages between users in near real time over persistent connections, supports 1:1 and group conversations, stores history, and syncs across devices.
- [Design a collaborative editor (Google Docs-like)](case-studies/design-collaborative-editor.md): Several users edit the same document at once, each seeing their own typing instantly and everyone else's within a fraction of a second, and all copies must converge to the same content without anyone's edits being lost.
- [Design a file sync service (Dropbox-like)](case-studies/design-file-sync.md): Users drop files into a folder on one device and the same tree appears on their other devices and on the web, with sharing and version history.
- [Design a distributed job scheduler](case-studies/design-job-scheduler.md): A job scheduler stores job definitions (one-off at a time, delayed, or recurring on a cron schedule), triggers each run when it is due, hands it to a worker, retries failures and records the outcome.
- [Design a distributed key-value store](case-studies/design-key-value-store.md): A distributed key-value store exposes `put(key, value)` and `get(key)` over a cluster, partitioning data across nodes and replicating each key for durability and availability.
- [Design a metrics and logging pipeline](case-studies/design-metrics-logging-pipeline.md): An observability platform collects **metrics** (numeric time series), **logs** (timestamped events) and often traces from every host and service, ships them through a buffered pipeline, stores them in purpose-built stores, and serves dashboards, queries and alerts.
- [Design a news feed](case-studies/design-news-feed.md): A news feed shows each user a reverse-chronological or ranked list of recent posts from accounts they follow.
- [Design a notification system](case-studies/design-notification-system.md): A notification platform accepts "notify this user about X" requests from internal services and delivers them over push (APNs, FCM), SMS, email and in-app channels.
- [Design a payment system](case-studies/design-payment-system.md): A payment system moves money on behalf of a merchant or platform: it takes a customer's payment instrument, authorises and captures funds through a payment service provider (PSP) or acquirer, records everything in an auditable ledger, and reconciles with external statements.
- [Design an LLM-backed RAG chat product](case-studies/design-rag-chat.md): A chat product where users ask questions in natural language and get answers grounded in a private corpus (docs, tickets, wiki pages), with citations.
- [Design a rate limiter service](case-studies/design-rate-limiter.md): A shared service (or library plus shared store) that decides, per request, whether a caller identified by a key (user, API key, IP, tenant, route) is within its quota, and answers in a millisecond or two.
- [Design a ride-sharing service](case-studies/design-ride-sharing.md): A ride-sharing platform connects riders to nearby available drivers in real time.
- [Design search autocomplete (typeahead)](case-studies/design-search-autocomplete.md): As the user types, return the k most relevant completions for the current prefix (usually 5-10), fast enough to keep up with typing.
- [Design a ticket booking system with seat holds](case-studies/design-ticket-booking.md): Users browse an event, pick specific seats (or a quantity in a section), hold them for a few minutes while they pay, and receive tickets.
- [Design a URL shortener](case-studies/design-url-shortener.md): A service that turns a long URL into a short alias (`https://sho.rt/aZ3kP9q`) and redirects visitors who open the alias.
- [Design a video streaming platform](case-studies/design-video-streaming.md): A video platform lets creators upload videos, converts them into many renditions, and delivers them to viewers worldwide with adaptive bitrate streaming.
- [Design a web crawler](case-studies/design-web-crawler.md): A web crawler discovers and downloads pages by following links from seed URLs, feeding a search index, an ML corpus or an archive.

## data

- [Batch and stream processing](data/batch-and-stream-processing.md): Batch processing runs a computation over a bounded, complete dataset on a schedule (nightly report, model training, backfill).
- [Change data capture (CDC)](data/change-data-capture.md): Change data capture turns the committed changes of a database (inserts, updates, deletes) into an ordered stream that other systems consume: search indexes, caches, warehouses, other services.
- [Data modeling and schema design](data/data-modeling-and-schema-design.md): Schema design decides what your data can express and what bad states the database refuses to store.
- [Data warehousing and OLAP](data/data-warehousing-and-olap.md): OLTP databases serve many small transactional reads and writes; OLAP systems serve fewer, heavy analytical queries that scan and aggregate large volumes.
- [Database connection pooling](data/database-connection-pooling.md): A connection pool keeps a bounded set of open database connections and lends them to requests, so each request skips the TCP, TLS and authentication handshake and the database sees a controlled number of sessions.
- [Database indexing](data/database-indexing.md): An index is a separate, ordered (or hashed) structure that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table.
- [Graph databases](data/graph-databases.md): A graph database stores entities as nodes and relationships as first-class edges, and answers queries by walking edges (traversal) instead of joining tables.
- [ORMs and the N+1 query problem](data/orm-and-n-plus-one.md): An ORM maps rows to objects so code manipulates models instead of SQL strings.
- [Schema migrations](data/schema-migrations.md): A migration is a versioned, repeatable change to the database schema (and sometimes data), stored in source control and applied by tooling in order.
- [SQL vs NoSQL](data/sql-vs-nosql.md): "SQL" databases are relational systems with a fixed schema, joins, and ACID transactions.
- [Storage engines (B-tree and LSM-tree)](data/storage-engines-btree-lsm.md): A storage engine is the part of a database that lays bytes out on disk and finds them again.
- [Time-series databases](data/time-series-databases.md): A time-series database (TSDB) stores sequences of `(timestamp, value)` samples keyed by a series identity, and is built for one workload: a steady stream of appends of recent data, queries over time ranges, aggregation into buckets, and deletion of whole old ranges.
- [Transactions and isolation levels](data/transactions-and-isolation-levels.md): A transaction groups several operations so they succeed or fail together (atomicity) and, while running, appear isolated from concurrent work.
- [Vector databases for engineers](data/vector-databases-for-engineers.md): A vector database stores fixed-length float vectors (embeddings) with an id and metadata, and answers "the k nearest vectors to this query vector", usually with a metadata filter.

## design

- [Clean code and naming](design/clean-code-and-naming.md): Code is read many more times than it is written, so optimize for the next reader.
- [Coupling, cohesion and core design principles](design/coupling-cohesion-and-design-principles.md): Good design makes change cheap.
- [Dependency injection](design/dependency-injection.md): Dependency injection (DI) means a component receives its collaborators from outside instead of constructing or looking them up itself.
- [Design patterns (GoF) in practice](design/design-patterns-gof.md): Design patterns are named, reusable solutions to recurring design problems, mostly about reducing coupling and making variation explicit.
- [Error handling strategies](design/error-handling-strategies.md): Error handling is deciding, for each failure, who detects it, who can fix it, what the caller sees and what gets recorded.
- [Functional core, imperative shell](design/functional-core-imperative-shell.md): Split a program into a pure core that makes all the decisions from plain values, and a thin imperative shell that gathers inputs (DB, network, clock, files), calls the core, and carries out its results.
- [API design for libraries](design/library-api-design.md): A library's public API is a promise: once others depend on it, every name, parameter, default, exception and observable behavior is hard to change.
- [Refactoring and code smells](design/refactoring-and-code-smells.md): Refactoring is changing the internal structure of code without changing its observable behavior, in small steps, each verified by tests.
- [SOLID principles](design/solid-principles.md): Five heuristics for organizing classes and modules so that change stays local: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion.
- [State machines](design/state-machines.md): A finite state machine (FSM) models something that is always in exactly one of a fixed set of states and moves between them only through named transitions triggered by events.

## distributed-systems

- [CAP theorem and PACELC](distributed-systems/cap-and-pacelc.md): CAP says that when a network partition happens, a replicated system must choose between answering every request (availability) and answering them all correctly as if there were one copy (linearizable consistency).
- [Consensus (Raft and Paxos)](distributed-systems/consensus-raft-paxos.md): Consensus lets a group of nodes agree on a value (or an ordered log of values) even when some nodes crash and messages are delayed or lost, as long as a majority is alive and connected.
- [Consistency models](distributed-systems/consistency-models.md): A consistency model is a contract about which values a read may return given the history of writes across replicas and clients.
- [Consistent hashing](distributed-systems/consistent-hashing.md): Consistent hashing maps keys and nodes into the same hash space so that when a node is added or removed only about `1/N` of the keys move, instead of nearly all of them as with `hash(key) % N`.
- [Distributed locks and leader election](distributed-systems/distributed-locks-and-leader-election.md): A distributed lock gives one process at a time the right to act on a shared resource; leader election is the same thing held for a long time by one replica of a service.
- [Distributed transactions and sagas](distributed-systems/distributed-transactions-and-sagas.md): When one business operation spans several databases or services, you cannot rely on a single ACID transaction.
- [Failure modes and the fallacies of distributed computing](distributed-systems/failure-modes-and-fallacies.md): A distributed system is one where a computer you did not know existed can make your own work fail.
- [Gossip protocols and failure detection](distributed-systems/gossip-and-failure-detection.md): A gossip (epidemic) protocol spreads information by having each node periodically exchange state with a few randomly chosen peers, so an update reaches the whole cluster in a number of rounds that grows with the logarithm of the cluster size, with no coordinator and constant work per node.
- [Idempotency and exactly-once processing](distributed-systems/idempotency-and-exactly-once.md): Networks lose requests and responses, so clients and brokers retry, and the same operation arrives more than once.
- [Partitioning and sharding](distributed-systems/partitioning-and-sharding.md): Partitioning splits a dataset into disjoint pieces (partitions/shards), each stored on different nodes, so that storage, writes and queries scale beyond one machine.
- [Replication](distributed-systems/replication.md): Replication keeps copies of the same data on several nodes to survive failures, serve reads closer to users and add read throughput.
- [Time, clocks and ordering](distributed-systems/time-clocks-and-ordering.md): In a distributed system there is no shared clock, and wall clocks on different machines disagree and can jump.

## frontend

- [Accessibility basics](frontend/accessibility-basics.md): Accessibility (a11y) means people with visual, motor, hearing or cognitive disabilities can perceive, operate and understand your interface, often through assistive technology such as screen readers, switch devices or magnification.
- [Browser rendering and Core Web Vitals](frontend/browser-rendering-and-core-web-vitals.md): A browser turns HTML, CSS and JavaScript into pixels through the critical rendering path: parse HTML into the DOM, parse CSS into the CSSOM, combine them into a render tree, compute layout, paint and composite.
- [Internationalization and localization](frontend/internationalization-and-localization.md): Internationalization (i18n) is designing and building software so it can be adapted to different languages, regions and cultures without code changes; localization (l10n) is the adaptation itself for one target locale: translated text, local formats, and cultural fit.
- [Web performance](frontend/web-performance.md): Front-end performance work is mostly about sending fewer bytes, sending them once, and asking for the important ones first.

## fundamentals

- [Algorithm patterns (reusable problem-solving techniques)](fundamentals/algorithm-patterns.md): Most practical algorithm problems are variations on a dozen patterns.
- [Big-O complexity and cost analysis](fundamentals/big-o-complexity.md): Big-O describes how the cost (time or memory) of an operation grows with input size n, ignoring constants and lower-order terms.
- [Concurrency and parallelism](fundamentals/concurrency-and-parallelism.md): Concurrency is structuring a program as independently progressing tasks (dealing with many things at once); parallelism is executing tasks literally simultaneously on multiple cores.
- [Core data structures and when to pick each](fundamentals/core-data-structures.md): Most performance and correctness problems at the code level reduce to picking the wrong container.
- [CPU caches and the memory hierarchy](fundamentals/cpu-caches-and-memory-hierarchy.md): Storage is arranged in levels: registers, several levels of CPU cache, main memory, then SSD/disk and the network, each level larger and slower than the one above.
- [Graph algorithms](fundamentals/graph-algorithms.md): Many engineering problems are graphs in disguise: dependencies, networks, routes, social links, state transitions.
- [Memory and performance engineering](fundamentals/memory-and-performance.md): Performance work is a measurement discipline: find the real bottleneck with a profiler, change one thing, re-measure.
- [Networking fundamentals for application engineers](fundamentals/networking-fundamentals.md): Application engineers need a working model of the layers between code and wire: DNS resolves names, TCP (or QUIC) gives reliable streams, TLS secures them, HTTP carries requests.
- [OS processes, threads and I/O models](fundamentals/processes-threads-and-io-models.md): A process is an isolated address space with its own resources; a thread is a schedulable flow of execution inside a process that shares its memory.
- [Strings and text encoding](fundamentals/strings-and-text-encoding.md): Text is a sequence of Unicode code points; bytes are what files, sockets and databases store.

## practices

- [Agile, Scrum and Kanban](practices/agile-scrum-kanban.md): Agile is a set of values for delivering software in small increments with fast feedback; Scrum and Kanban are two concrete frameworks for it.
- [Architecture decision records (ADRs)](practices/architecture-decision-records.md): An ADR is a short, immutable document capturing one significant architectural decision: the context, the options considered, the choice made, and its consequences.
- [Code review](practices/code-review.md): Code review is a second engineer examining a change before it lands, to catch defects, keep the design coherent, spread knowledge and maintain shared standards.
- [Documentation practices](practices/documentation-practices.md): Good documentation lets someone other than the author use, operate and change the system without asking.
- [Estimation and planning](practices/estimation-and-planning.md): Estimation predicts effort or duration under uncertainty; planning turns those predictions into a sequenced, adjustable commitment.
- [Git workflows and branching](practices/git-workflows-and-branching.md): A branching workflow is the team agreement on where work happens, how it gets to the shared mainline, and how releases are cut.
- [Release versioning and changelogs](practices/release-versioning-and-changelogs.md): A version number is a message to users about what changed and whether upgrading is safe.
- [Technical debt management](practices/technical-debt-management.md): Technical debt is the future cost of past design and implementation shortcuts: extra effort every time you change the affected code.

## reliability

- [Backup and disaster recovery](reliability/backup-and-disaster-recovery.md): Backups protect against losing data (deletion, corruption, ransomware, a bad migration); disaster recovery (DR) is the plan and standby infrastructure that brings the whole service back after losing a site or region.
- [Capacity planning and autoscaling](reliability/capacity-planning-and-autoscaling.md): Capacity planning is predicting how much compute, memory, storage and network a system needs to meet its SLOs at forecast demand plus headroom; autoscaling adjusts that capacity automatically as load changes.
- [Chaos engineering and fault injection](reliability/chaos-engineering.md): Chaos engineering is running controlled experiments that inject real-world faults (killed instances, added latency, failing dependencies, lost zones) into a system to check a hypothesis that its steady-state behavior will hold.
- [CI/CD pipelines](reliability/ci-cd-pipelines.md): Continuous integration merges and verifies small changes frequently with automated build and test; continuous delivery keeps every green main-branch commit deployable, and continuous deployment ships it to production automatically.
- [Containers and Docker](reliability/containers-and-docker.md): A container is a regular Linux process isolated with namespaces and limited with cgroups, started from an immutable layered image that bundles the app and its userspace dependencies.
- [Deployment strategies - rolling, blue-green, canary, feature flags](reliability/deployment-strategies.md): A deployment strategy defines how a new version replaces the old one and how you limit the damage if it is bad.
- [Feature flags](reliability/feature-flags.md): A feature flag (feature toggle) is a runtime decision point that switches code paths without redeploying, which separates deploying code from releasing behavior.
- [Health checks and graceful shutdown](reliability/health-checks-and-graceful-shutdown.md): Health checks tell the platform (load balancer, Kubernetes, service mesh) whether an instance should receive traffic and whether it should be restarted; graceful shutdown lets an instance leave without dropping the requests it already accepted.
- [Incident response and postmortems](reliability/incident-response-and-postmortems.md): Incident response is a rehearsed process for detecting, coordinating, mitigating and communicating during a production problem; the postmortem is the blameless written review afterwards that turns the failure into lasting fixes.
- [Infrastructure as code](reliability/infrastructure-as-code.md): Infrastructure as code (IaC) defines servers, networks, databases, permissions and clusters in versioned text files that tools apply automatically and repeatably.
- [Kubernetes basics](reliability/kubernetes-basics.md): Kubernetes is a declarative container orchestrator: you describe desired state (N replicas of this image, exposed on this port) and controllers continuously reconcile reality toward it, scheduling, restarting, scaling and rolling out workloads across a cluster of nodes.
- [Multi-region architecture (active-passive, active-active, cells)](reliability/multi-region-architecture.md): Multi-region architecture runs a service in two or more geographically separate cloud regions so it survives the loss of a region and serves distant users with lower latency.
- [Observability - logs, metrics, traces](reliability/observability-logs-metrics-traces.md): Observability is the ability to ask new questions about a running system from the telemetry it emits, without shipping new code.
- [Resilience patterns - timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads](reliability/resilience-patterns.md): In a distributed system dependencies will be slow or down; resilience patterns keep a partial failure from becoming a total one.
- [SLIs, SLOs and error budgets](reliability/slis-slos-error-budgets.md): An SLI is a measured indicator of service health from the user's perspective (for example the fraction of requests that succeed fast enough).

## scenarios

- [Background jobs and queues - choosing an approach](scenarios/background-jobs-and-queues.md): Anything the user does not need to wait for should leave the request path: accept the request, record the work durably, return, and let a worker do it.
- [Choosing a caching strategy](scenarios/choosing-a-caching-strategy.md): Decide three things in order: whether to cache at all (measure and fix the query first), at which layer (browser/HTTP, CDN, in-process, distributed cache, materialised view), and how staleness is bounded (TTL, explicit invalidation, versioned keys, or validation with ETags).
- [Choosing a database](scenarios/choosing-a-database.md): Pick the database by access patterns, consistency needs, data shape and scale, in that order, then by team familiarity and operational cost.
- [Choosing a multi-tenancy model](scenarios/choosing-a-multi-tenancy-model.md): Multi-tenancy serves many customers (tenants) from shared software.
- [Choosing an auth approach](scenarios/choosing-an-auth-approach.md): Split the question in three: who is the caller (a person in a browser, a mobile app, another service, a third-party developer), who proves their identity (you, or an identity provider), and how the proof travels on each request (session cookie, access token, API key, client certificate).
- [Choosing a communication style](scenarios/choosing-communication-style.md): Decide along two axes: does the caller need the answer now (synchronous request/response) or can work happen later (asynchronous messaging and events), and who are the consumers (public, internal, browsers)?
- [Choosing file and media storage](scenarios/choosing-file-and-media-storage.md): Put file bytes in object storage and file metadata (owner, key, size, type, status) in your database.
- [Choosing real-time updates - polling vs SSE vs WebSockets](scenarios/choosing-realtime-updates.md): Pick by direction, frequency and who the receiver is.
- [Migrating a monolith to services](scenarios/migrating-monolith-to-services.md): Migrate incrementally, one capability at a time, and only for a stated reason (team contention, different scaling or isolation needs), never as a rewrite.
- [Scaling from zero to millions of users](scenarios/scaling-from-zero-to-millions.md): Scale in stages, each triggered by a measured bottleneck, not in advance.
- [Scenario chooser - what approach for X](scenarios/scenario-chooser.md): A router from concrete problems and requirements to the topic files that answer them.

## security

- [Authentication and sessions](security/authentication-and-sessions.md): Authentication proves who a caller is; a session carries that proof across requests.
- [Authorization models (RBAC, ABAC, ReBAC)](security/authorization-models.md): Authorization decides whether an authenticated principal may perform an action on a resource.
- [Browser security - same-origin policy, CORS, CSP and security headers](security/browser-security-cors-csp-headers.md): Browsers run code from many sites side by side, so they enforce the same-origin policy: script from one origin cannot read responses or DOM from another.
- [Cryptography and TLS](security/cryptography-and-tls.md): Applied cryptography for engineers is mostly about choosing the right primitive, using a vetted library with safe defaults, and managing keys.
- [OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect](security/oauth2-and-oidc.md): OAuth 2.0 is a delegation framework: a user (resource owner) lets a client application obtain a limited access token for an API without sharing their password.
- [OWASP Top 10 (2025 edition)](security/owasp-top-10.md): The OWASP Top 10 is a consensus awareness list of the most critical web application security risks.
- [Privacy and PII handling](security/privacy-and-pii-handling.md): Personal data is any information about an identifiable person, and handling it well is mostly an engineering problem: collect less, know where it lives, restrict and encrypt it, keep it out of logs, delete it on schedule and on request.
- [Secrets management](security/secrets-management.md): Secrets are credentials that grant access: API keys, DB passwords, signing keys, tokens, certificates.
- [Software supply chain security](security/software-supply-chain-security.md): Your software is mostly other people's code, built by tools and pipelines you also did not write.
- [Threat modeling](security/threat-modeling.md): Threat modeling is structured thinking about what can go wrong in a system before (and while) it is built, so security work targets real risks and is cheap to act on.

## system-design

- [API gateway and service mesh](system-design/api-gateway-and-service-mesh.md): An **API gateway** is the single entry point for external (north-south) traffic: routing, authentication, rate limiting, TLS termination, request shaping.
- [Back-of-envelope estimation](system-design/back-of-envelope-estimation.md): Quick order-of-magnitude arithmetic that turns "100M users" into QPS, storage and bandwidth so you can pick an architecture on evidence.
- [Blob and object storage](system-design/blob-object-storage.md): Object storage (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob, MinIO, Ceph) stores immutable-ish blobs addressed by key in flat buckets, accessed over HTTP.
- [Caching strategies](system-design/caching-strategies.md): A cache stores the result of expensive work (DB query, computation, remote call) in faster memory to cut latency and backend load.
- [CDN and edge](system-design/cdn-and-edge.md): A content delivery network is a globally distributed set of cache servers (points of presence, PoPs) that serve content from a location near the user and shield the origin.
- [Load balancing](system-design/load-balancing.md): A load balancer (LB) distributes incoming requests across a pool of backends, removes failed backends via health checks, and gives clients a single stable address.
- [Message queues and streams](system-design/message-queues-and-streams.md): Messaging systems move data asynchronously between producers and consumers.
- [Probabilistic data structures (Bloom filter, Count-Min Sketch, HyperLogLog)](system-design/probabilistic-data-structures.md): Probabilistic data structures (sketches) answer membership, frequency and distinct-count questions over huge sets or streams in a small, fixed amount of memory, in exchange for a bounded, tunable error.
- [Rate limiting](system-design/rate-limiting.md): Rate limiting caps how much work a client (user, API key, IP, tenant) can request per unit time.
- [Realtime with WebSockets, SSE and polling](system-design/realtime-websockets-sse.md): HTTP is request/response, so servers cannot spontaneously push to a client.
- [Search systems](system-design/search-systems.md): A search system answers free-text queries over a corpus by building an **inverted index** (term to the list of documents containing it) and ranking matches by relevance (TF-IDF/BM25 plus business signals).
- [System design interview framework](system-design/system-design-interview-framework.md): A repeatable sequence for designing a large system from an ambiguous prompt: clarify requirements, estimate scale, sketch a high-level design, deep-dive the hard parts, then discuss bottlenecks and trade-offs.
- [Unique ID generation](system-design/unique-id-generation.md): Every entity needs an identifier that is unique, cheap to produce, and ideally well behaved in the database index.

## testing

- [Flaky test handling](testing/flaky-tests.md): A flaky test passes and fails on the same code.
- [Integration and contract testing](testing/integration-and-contract-testing.md): Integration tests check that your code works with real collaborators: database, message broker, filesystem, HTTP framework.
- [Mutation testing](testing/mutation-testing.md): Mutation testing measures how good your tests are by deliberately introducing small bugs (mutants) into the code, such as flipping `<` to `<=` or replacing `+` with `-`, and running the suite against each one.
- [Performance and load testing](testing/performance-and-load-testing.md): Performance testing measures how a system behaves under load: throughput, latency percentiles, error rate and resource use.
- [Property-based and fuzz testing](testing/property-based-and-fuzz-testing.md): Property-based testing states a rule that must hold for all inputs (a *property*) and lets a framework generate hundreds of inputs, then shrinks any failure to a minimal counterexample.
- [Snapshot and golden-file testing](testing/snapshot-and-golden-testing.md): A snapshot (golden-file, approval) test runs code, serializes its output, and compares it to a stored reference that a human approved earlier.
- [Static analysis, linting and type checking](testing/static-analysis-and-type-checking.md): Static analysis examines source code without running it to find bugs, style violations, security issues and type errors.
- [TDD and BDD](testing/tdd-and-bdd.md): Test-driven development (TDD) is a design and implementation loop: write a failing test, make it pass with the simplest code, then refactor.
- [Test data management](testing/test-data-management.md): Test data management is how tests get the inputs and stored state they need: building objects, seeding databases, and isolating each test's data from every other test's.
- [Testing strategy and the test pyramid](testing/testing-strategy-and-pyramid.md): A testing strategy decides which kinds of tests you write, in what proportions, and what each is responsible for, so that the suite gives fast, trustworthy feedback at a sustainable maintenance cost.
- [Unit testing and test doubles](testing/unit-testing-and-test-doubles.md): A unit test exercises a small piece of behaviour in isolation, fast and deterministically, and fails for exactly one reason.

- [Glossary](glossary.md): terms linked to the topic that explains each
